opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that AI is becoming the interface through which we interact with everything: how we find information, how we communicate, how we transact, eventually how we make decisions. If that layer is owned by a handful of companies whose business model is fundamentally about capturing your attention or monetizing your data, then the AI isn't really working for you. It's working for them, and you're the product.

We've already seen this play out with social media and search. The incentives drift over time. Even with good intentions at the start, once you're a public company optimizing for revenue, the system slowly gets tuned toward engagement, toward ads, toward keeping you inside the walled garden. With AI the stakes are much higher, because these systems will know far more about us. They'll have our health data, our finances, our private conversations, our goals. And they'll be acting on our behalf as agents.

So user-owned AI means a few things. First, the model and the agent should be aligned with the user's interests, provably, not just by a policy promise. Second, your data should stay under your control. You decide what's shared, and you can verify how it's used, which is where things like confidential computing and secure enclaves come in. Third, the economic value should flow back to the people who contribute data, compute, and models, rather than accumulating at a single chokepoint.

My background is on the research side. I worked on the Transformer paper at Google, so I've seen how fast the capabilities are moving. Then with NEAR, we spent years building infrastructure for open, permissionless systems where users own their assets and identity. User-owned AI is really the convergence of those two worlds. If we don't build this alternative now, while the architecture of the AI economy is still being set, we'll end up locked into a very centralized outcome that's hard to undo.

r001.rationale: The response warns about centralized ownership and incentives, but does not connect that concentration to a shift from open research toward secrecy.

r002.rationale: It says AI has higher stakes and may act on users’ behalf, but does not compare centralized AI control with centralized internet control.

r003.rationale: It describes AI as an interface for finding information and making decisions, but does not say dominant companies could shape how people think through that control.

r004.rationale: It advocates user-owned AI and mentions NEAR’s open, permissionless infrastructure, but does not identify blockchain-based ownership as the foundation.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention computational overhead from cryptographic safeguards as a barrier to applying them to machine learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it is that AI is increasingly going to be the layer through which people interact with information, with services, with each other. It's going to be mediating a lot of our lives. And right now the trajectory we're on is that this layer is owned by a handful of very large companies. These models are trained on effectively all of humanity's data, but the control over them, the economics around them, the decisions about what they optimize for, all of that sits with a few entities.

And the problem with that isn't theoretical. We've already lived through one version of it with social media and the internet platforms. You get these systems that are nominally free, but the actual business model is optimizing for engagement, for ad revenue, for whatever the shareholders need that quarter. And the user's interests end up being secondary at best. With AI the stakes are much higher, because it's not just what content you see, it's the assistant that's helping you make decisions, manage your finances, your health, how you learn. If that assistant is ultimately serving someone else's incentives, that's a pretty uncomfortable place to be.

So user-owned AI, to me, means a few things. One is that the model itself should be genuinely aligned with the user, not with the provider. Your AI should be working for you, and you should be able to verify that. Second is privacy, meaning your data and your interactions shouldn't be leaking into someone else's training set or someone else's business. And third is the economics. If these models are built on everyone's collective contributions, there should be a way for the value to flow back to the people contributing, whether that's data, compute, or the work of actually building and improving the models.

And coming from my background, both the Transformer work and then what we've been doing at NEAR, the piece that I think is actually tractable now is the infrastructure. You can have open models, you can have verifiable compute, you can have confidential execution so that you know what code is running and that nobody is looking at your data, and you can have decentralized coordination for who gets paid for what. The pieces exist. The question is whether we put them together in a way that gives individuals real ownership, or whether we just default into the centralized version because it's the path of least resistance.

I think it's important because this is one of those moments where the architecture of the technology sets the power structure for decades. We have a window to get it right, and I don't think we should assume the incentives of the big labs will take care of it for us.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI control concentrated among a few large companies, but does not attribute that concentration to a shift from open research toward secrecy.

r002.rationale: It says AI raises higher stakes than internet platforms because an assistant can help people make decisions about finances, health, and learning.

r003.rationale: The response says AI mediates interactions with information and decisions, but does not clearly warn that companies could shape how people think through control of that processing.

r004.rationale: It supports user ownership and mentions decentralized coordination, but does not propose blockchain-based ownership as its foundation.

r005.rationale: It presents cryptographic safeguards as tractable infrastructure and does not identify their computational overhead as a barrier.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is, who does your AI actually work for? As AI becomes more capable, it’s going to have access to more of your information and make more decisions on your behalf. If that AI is controlled by a company with its own incentives, those incentives may not align with yours.

User-owned AI means you have control over your data, over what the AI can do, and over who it interacts with. You should be able to move between services without losing the knowledge and context that make your assistant useful to you.

And there’s a broader economic question. If AI creates a huge amount of value, we want people to participate in that value, rather than have all of it concentrate in a few companies. So for me, this is about making AI something that gives people more agency—something that works for them and that they can actually control.

r001.rationale: The response discusses company incentives and value concentrating in a few companies, but does not connect that concentration to a shift from open research toward secrecy.

r002.rationale: It says AI may make decisions on users’ behalf, but does not compare the danger of centralized AI control with centralized internet control.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI access to information, but does not warn that dominant companies could shape how people think through AI-mediated information processing.

r004.rationale: It advocates user control and ownership of AI, data, and capabilities, but does not propose blockchain as the foundation.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention cryptographic safeguards, their computational overhead, or their applicability to machine learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI is going to become the interface through which we interact with a lot of the world. It will have context about who you are, what you care about, your work, your relationships, and it will increasingly take actions on your behalf. So the question is: who does that AI actually work for?

If it’s controlled by a company whose business is advertising or selling you things, its incentives may not line up with yours. You want an assistant that helps you accomplish your goals, and you want control over the information you share with it and what it’s allowed to do.

User-owned AI is about putting that control in the hands of the user. It doesn’t mean everybody has to train their own model. It means you can choose models and services, move your data, and decide who gets access. As these systems become more capable, that ownership becomes much more consequential, because you’re effectively delegating decisions to them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses company incentives and user control, but does not describe a shift from open research toward secrecy or argue that this shift concentrates control.

r002.rationale: It says users will delegate decisions to AI, but does not compare centralized AI control with centralized internet control or claim AI is more dangerous.

r003.rationale: It mentions a company with advertising or sales incentives, but does not warn that a handful of dominant companies could shape how people think through control of AI-mediated information.

r004.rationale: It advocates user ownership and control, but does not propose blockchain as its foundation.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention cryptographic safeguards or their computational overhead as a barrier for machine learning.
